followUps:
On a repeat visit the browser can skip DNS, the connection setup and often the whole request. The browser caches the DNS answer, so no lookup is needed. It may keep the TCP and TLS connection open and reuse it, saving about two to three round trips. Cached files with a fresh max-age are used straight from disk with no network at all.

Stale files are only revalidated with a small request that can return 304. TLS session resumption also makes any new handshake cheaper.

A CDN is a set of servers near users that answers on behalf of your origin server. DNS (or anycast routing) sends the browser to a nearby edge, so the TCP and TLS round trips are short. If the edge has the file cached it replies immediately, and your origin never sees the request.

Example: a 150 ms round trip to a far origin becomes about 20 ms to an edge, and three round trips save roughly 390 ms. The edge also compresses files and speaks HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 even if the origin does not.

HTTP/3 keeps the same requests, methods and status codes but swaps TCP for QUIC, which runs over UDP. The browser finds out through an Alt-Svc header or DNS record and may first use HTTP/2, then switch. QUIC includes TLS 1.3, so a new connection needs one round trip instead of two to three, and a repeat visit can use 0-RTT.

Each stream recovers from packet loss on its own, so one lost packet no longer stalls every download. Connections also survive a switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

code.title: Validate on the server: ignore the client's price

followUps:
A classic bug is a shop that trusts the price sent by the browser. The form shows 50 dollars, but someone edits the request with DevTools or curl and sends price: 0.01. If the server saves that value, the attacker buys a 50 dollar item for one cent. The same happens with a hidden isAdmin: true field or a quantity of -3, which creates a refund.

The fix is to look up the price on the server and ignore any price in the request.

Client-side validation is worth keeping because it gives instant feedback and saves a round trip. A user who mistypes an email sees the error as they type, instead of waiting a second for the server to say no. It also reduces useless traffic: if 20 percent of submissions would have failed, those never reach your server.

It is a usability feature, not a security feature, so the server must repeat every check. Use both: client for speed, server for truth.

code.title: Parse a URL and compare origins

followUps:
No, they are different origins. The origin is scheme plus host plus port, and the host must match exactly, so a.com and www.a.com differ. A page on one cannot read responses from the other with fetch unless the server sends CORS headers.

The program shows that https://a.com versus http://a.com also differs (scheme), and a different port would too. Cookies are more relaxed: a cookie with Domain=a.com is sent to both hosts.

Never paste the value into the string by hand. Percent-encode it, so & becomes %26, otherwise the server reads it as the start of a new parameter. Use URLSearchParams or encodeURIComponent.

const p = new URLSearchParams();
p.set("q", "salt & pepper");
p.toString(); // "q=salt+%26+pepper"
encodeURIComponent("a&b"); // "a%26b"

The server decodes it back to salt & pepper. Spaces become + or %20.

Retry only requests that can be repeated without harm: idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) that failed with a temporary problem. Safe status codes to retry are 408, 429 (wait for the Retry-After value), 502, 503 and 504. A plain 500 is risky because the server may have done part of the work.

Never retry 400, 401, 403 or 404: the same request will fail again. Use exponential backoff with jitter, for example waits of 1 s, 2 s, 4 s plus a random amount.

Return 422 Unprocessable Content (or 400 Bad Request) with a JSON body that says which fields failed and why, so the form can show each message next to its field. 409 fits a conflict such as a duplicate email.

HTTP/1.1 422
{"errors": [
  {"field": "email", "message": "must contain @"},
  {"field": "qty", "message": "must be 1 to 10"}
]}

Do not return 200 with an error inside, because caches and monitoring would treat it as success.

The HTML source is the text file the server sent. The DOM is the live tree of objects the browser builds from it, and it can differ from the source. The parser fixes mistakes, for example adding a missing <tbody> inside a table, and JavaScript can add, remove or change nodes afterwards.

Example: the source has an empty <ul>, then a script appends 3 <li> items. View Source still shows an empty list, but Elements in DevTools shows 3 items. Crawlers that skip JavaScript see only the source.

If JavaScript fails to load, everything that depends on it stops, but the HTML and CSS still work. Links navigate, plain forms submit and text is readable. A page built only with a script that fills an empty <div id="root"> shows a blank screen instead.

Failures are common: a flaky mobile network, an ad blocker, a CDN outage or a syntax error in one bundle. Put essential content in HTML, and put a <noscript> message or server rendering in place so users still get something.

The preload scanner is a second, lightweight parser that reads ahead in the HTML while the main parser is blocked on a script or stylesheet. It spots <img>, <link> and <script src> tags early and starts those downloads in parallel, so the network is not idle.

It cannot see resources that JavaScript adds later or CSS background-image URLs found only after the file loads. Put important files in the HTML or add <link rel="preload"> for them.

LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) is usually one hero image or heading, so first find which element it is in the Performance panel or Lighthouse. Then attack its four parts: slow server (TTFB), late discovery, slow download and slow render.

  • Cache HTML at a CDN to cut TTFB.
  • Put the hero image in the HTML with fetchpriority="high", not lazy-loaded.
  • Serve a right-sized AVIF or WebP; 800 KB down to 120 KB saves about 1.4 s on a 4G link.
  • Inline critical CSS and defer scripts.

Changing transform or opacity does not change any element's size or position in the document, so the browser skips layout and paint. It only asks the GPU compositor to move or fade a layer that is already drawn, which is cheap and can run off the main thread.

Animating left, width or margin forces layout of the page again every frame, plus paint. At 60 fps there are only about 16 ms per frame, so use transform: translateX(...) for movement instead.

code.title: When classic, async and deferred scripts run

followUps:
Deferred scripts fire before DOMContentLoaded: the browser runs them after parsing ends and before it fires that event. Module scripts do too, because they are deferred by default. Async scripts have no guarantee. One may run before parsing finishes, or after DOMContentLoaded if it downloads slowly.

The program above prints the order: the classic script and the async script run during parsing, parsing finishes, the deferred scripts run in order, and then DOMContentLoaded fires.

It breaks unpredictably, because the async script runs whenever it arrives, while the deferred one waits for parsing. If the deferred script needs a library from the async one and the library is slow, the deferred script runs first and throws an error like $ is not defined. It works on your fast laptop and fails on a slow phone.

Fix it by making both deferred (they keep document order), by using ES modules with import, which handles the dependency for you, or by removing async from the library.

Yes, it can. First paint depends on CSS being ready and something to draw, not on images or fonts finishing. In normal pages it happens well before load. But if the page body is empty until a script runs, or a script blocks rendering, first paint may happen later than load or never be a useful one.

Example: a page with a 2 MB script that fills an empty div can fire load at 1.5 s but only paint real content at 2.5 s. This is why first paint is measured separately.

document.readyState tells you which stage the document is at: "loading" while parsing, "interactive" once parsing is done, and "complete" when everything has loaded. DOMContentLoaded fires when it becomes "interactive" (after deferred scripts) and load when it becomes "complete".

if (document.readyState === "loading") {
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", init);
} else {
  init(); // event already fired
}

code.title: fetch wrapper that throws on HTTP errors

followUps:
Create an AbortController for each request, and abort the previous one before sending a new one. The old fetch then rejects with an AbortError, which you ignore.

let ctrl;
async function search(q) {
  if (ctrl) ctrl.abort();
  ctrl = new AbortController();
  const r = await fetch(url + q, { signal: ctrl.signal });
  return r.json();
}

This stops an older, slower answer from replacing the newer one. Debouncing the input by about 250 ms also cuts the request count.

A retry can run the action twice. If the first POST reached the server and created an order, but the response was lost on the way back, the client sees a failure, retries and creates a second order. The customer is charged twice.

POST is not idempotent by default. To make it safe, send an Idempotency-Key header with a unique value per action. The server stores the result for that key and returns the same response for a repeat, instead of doing the work again.

A preflight is an automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a cross-origin request that is not "simple". For example, a request with Content-Type: application/json or an Authorization header triggers it. It asks whether the real request is allowed.

The server answers with headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers. If they do not match, the browser blocks the real request. Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the answer, avoiding an extra round trip each time.

It means the browser answered from its own cache, with no network request at all. It is the fastest possible result, often 0 to 2 ms. It is shown as "(memory cache)" for the current page session and "(disk cache)" for files stored on disk from earlier visits.

It is not the same as a 304, which still makes a small round trip to ask the server. Tick Disable cache when measuring first-visit speed, or you will see numbers that real new users never get.

Your laptop on office Wi-Fi is much faster than a typical user, so measure real users (RUM). Add the web-vitals library, send LCP, INP and CLS values to an analytics endpoint, and group them by device, country and connection type.

Look at the 75th percentile, not the average, as Google's CrUX data does. Example: 10 visits of 1 s and 1 visit of 10 s average 1.8 s, but the p75 is 1 s and the p95 shows the pain. Compare field data with lab tests to find gaps.

code.title: Browser cache: fresh, 304 and full download

followUps:
Users get stuck on the old page. A response with max-age=31536000 is reused for a year with no request, so after you deploy, browsers keep showing the old HTML, which points to old bundle filenames. You cannot recall a copy in someone's browser; users would have to clear their cache.

That is why HTML gets no-cache plus an ETag, so each visit asks quickly, while the fingerprinted files can be cached for a year. The fingerprint (hash) in the filename is what makes a year safe.

A CDN is a shared cache that also obeys Cache-Control. s-maxage sets freshness for shared caches only, so you can keep the CDN copy for an hour while browsers use max-age=0. private tells the CDN not to store a user-specific response; public allows it.

The CDN adds an Age header showing how old its copy is. Vary makes it keep one copy per header value, for example per Accept-Encoding. After a deploy, purge or use new filenames.

Cache busting means changing a file's URL when its content changes, so the browser must download it again. The best method is fingerprinting: put a hash of the content in the filename, such as app.3f9a1c.js, which your build tool generates. A new build makes app.8be204.js, a URL the browser has never seen.

A weaker method is a query string, app.js?v=12, which some caches ignore. Fingerprinting lets you cache files for a year safely.

Server push let the server send files before the browser asked for them, but it usually wasted bandwidth. The server could not know what the browser already had cached, so it pushed files that were already stored, and the push often competed with the pages' important files. Setting it up correctly was hard and gains were small or negative.

Chrome removed support in 2022. Use <link rel="preload"> or 103 Early Hints instead, since the browser can then decide with its own cache knowledge.

103 Early Hints is an interim response the server sends while it is still preparing the real answer. It carries Link headers such as </app.css>; rel=preload, so the browser starts downloading CSS and fonts during the server's "think time".

Example: the HTML takes 300 ms to generate. With Early Hints the browser fetches the CSS in those 300 ms, instead of waiting to read it from the HTML. The final 200 response then arrives as usual. It works through CDNs that support it.

Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, right-click the column header and enable the Protocol column. It shows http/1.1, h2 or h3 for each request. You can also look at the response headers in the request details, or run curl -I --http3 if your curl supports it.

Do not be surprised if the first visit shows h2 and later ones h3: the browser learns about HTTP/3 from Alt-Svc after the first response.

Choose by how often the content changes and how personal it is. SSG (pages built at deploy time) suits stable pages like a blog and gives the fastest result from a CDN edge near the user. SSR (HTML built per request) suits personalised or fresh pages but needs a nearby server, or it adds delay. CSR (a blank page plus JavaScript) is the worst fit here: low-end phones must download and run the bundle first.

A good mix is SSG or cached SSR for public pages, plus client code only where it is interactive.

A performance budget is a limit a build must not exceed, checked in CI. Example for this audience: JavaScript at most 170 KB compressed, LCP under 2.5 s on Slow 4G with a mid-range phone, INP under 200 ms, and total page weight under 1 MB.

// size check in CI
if (bundleKB > 170) {
  console.error("over budget");
  process.exit(1);
}

Tools such as Lighthouse CI can enforce these. A failing check blocks the merge, so regressions are caught before users feel them.

Treat third-party scripts as guests with strict limits. Load them with async or defer, or after the page is interactive. Remove those nobody uses, and review each new tag for its cost. Measure each one: a chat widget costing 300 KB and 400 ms of main-thread time on a low-end phone may not be worth it.

Options include a facade (a fake button that loads the real widget on click), self-hosting, a tag manager with approval, and a budget that fails CI when added weight passes a limit.
